Simple Example.

You hear some rumors that a new highway off-ramp may be built in a remote area. If it's built the land values around that off-ramp will skyrocket. But if the ramp isn't built, that land will still be worthless. So you find out who owns the land, and you buy a future from them. You pay them a fee for the ability to purchase the land for a set amount over a period of time. So if the land is currently worth $100,000, you pay them $10,000 to purchase the land at any time over the next 3 years for $500,000. If the interchange isn't built, you are out $10,000. If it is, and the land is now valued at $1,000,000, you can purchase it for $500,000.

To Short a Future is basically the opposite. Say you own $100,000 worth of land, and you hear that they may put in a garbage dump next door. That would dramatically lower your land value. So you buy a future from an investor for $5,000. But this being a "Short" the deal is that at any time in the next 3 years the investor MUST purchase the land from you if you "call in the Short" for $50,000. So if the dump is not built, You are out $5,000. But if it is built and your land is now worthless, You can make the call and get $50,000.

On both ends the person who owns the land or commodity is participating in the deal. And in both cases the market is determining the true price of the (asset).
